name: Casing At A Third Of The Width It Should Be
aka: ranch casing on a classical opening
symptom: The band of trim around an opening is 2 1/4 or 3 1/2 in wide where the classical rule asks for a sixth to a fifth of the opening — 6 to 7 1/5 in on a 36 in opening. The surround reads as an outline rather than as a frame, and every classical element that is supposed to be measured against it, from the door entablature to the interior chair rail, loses its reference. Modern practice misses this by roughly a factor of three.

cause.explanation: Casing is a milled profile sold by the linear foot in a small number of stock widths, and the two that dominate the market — 2 1/4 in colonial and 3 1/2 in — were set by twentieth-century economy and have been reinforced by every jamb, every pre-hung door unit and every corner-block system since. A 6 in casing is a special order in most markets. There is also a jamb-depth driver: wide casing wants a proportionally deeper backband and a jamb extension, and every pre-hung assembly is dimensioned around narrow trim.
cause.cost_saved: Roughly 1.20 to 2.50 USD a linear foot for stock against 4 to 9 USD for wide profiled casing, plus the mitre and backband labour. On a whole house, 3,000 to 12,000 USD, which is why it is the interior line item most often cut.

rule_violated.statement: casing width = opening_width / 6, which is 6 in on a 36 in opening; Palladio permits 1/6 to 1/5 of the void.
window casing = opening_width / 5.5, which is 6 9/16 in — the window casing is WIDER than the door casing in the same room.
casing projection = opening_width / 6 * 0.18, about 1 1/16 in. Width without projection is only half the rule.
module / 6 = 6 in, with the full entablature above at three times that, 18 in.

correct_practice: Casing width = opening width / 6 to / 5. On a 36 in opening that is 6 to 7 1/5 in; on a 30 in opening 5 to 6 in; on a 42 in door 7 to 8 2/5 in. The window casing in a given room is wider than the door casing in the same room, at opening / 5.5 against opening / 6, because the window is the thing being framed and the door is the thing being passed through. Projection about 0.18 of the casing width, roughly 1 in on a 6 in casing, which normally means a backband. The exterior head assembly above a window runs about 2.6 times the casing width in total height. Federal work narrows the casing deliberately and Greek Revival broadens it, and the pack's own invariants check that ordering.

fixes.right: Wide casing at opening / 6 with a backband, mitred or with corner blocks according to the family. Order the jambs to suit.
fixes.cheap: Build the width out of stock. A 3 1/2 in stock casing with a 1 1/4 in backband and a 1 in outer strip reaches 5 3/4 in with no special milling, three cuts, and material that is on the shelf. The profile will not be as good as a run one; the width and the projection, which are what the eye measures, will be right. Width first, profile second — this is the correct order of concession and almost everyone gets it backwards.
fixes.dishonest: A wider flat board with no backband and no projection. This gets the plan dimension right and leaves the section flat, so the surround now reads as a broad pale stripe. The projection is doing at least half the work; a 6 in flat board is not obviously better than a 3 1/2 in profiled one.

detection: Measure the casing width against the opening width in a photograph. Below 0.14 (that is, narrower than opening / 7) the fault is present; the stock 2 1/4 in casing on a 36 in opening gives 0.06, against the correct 0.167. Second test: compare the window casing with the door casing in the same room — if they are identical, the trim was bought rather than composed. Third: look at the outer edge of the casing for a backband shadow; a flat outer edge meeting the wall with no step means the projection rule is unmet as well.

exceptions.why: The style refuses casing almost entirely — its own constraint caps it at 3 in and 1 in of projection, and openings are meant to read as punched.
exceptions.bounds: The refusal must be systematic: no corner boards, no projecting heads, no moulded sills, shingles over corners. A house that takes this licence at the windows and then applies a classical entry with pilasters has not understood it.

bounds_test.note: 3 in on a 36 in opening is 0.083. The refusal must be systematic: no corner boards, no projecting heads, no moulded sills, shingles over corners.

exceptions.why: The type caps window casing at 4 to 5 in as a deliberate budget that must read as a budget, with no continuous frieze and no pilasters.
exceptions.bounds: 4 to 5 in flat with a drip cap over. Below 4 in the type stops reading as a nineteenth-century building; above 5 in it starts claiming a rank it does not have.

bounds_test.note: 4 to 5 in, with no continuous frieze and no pilasters. Below 4 in the type stops reading as a nineteenth-century building; above 5 in it claims a rank it does not have.

exceptions.why: Broad, flat, unmoulded trim is the style's method — ornament by profile and mass rather than by relief carving — and the casing is deliberately wider than Georgian at 7 to 9 in.
exceptions.bounds: Broad AND flat is licensed here; narrow and flat is not. The Greek Revival casing exceeds opening / 5, which is the top of Palladio's band, and that excess is the style's argument.

bounds_test.note: Broad AND flat is licensed; narrow and flat is not. The Greek Revival casing exceeds Palladio's upper bound at 7 to 9 in on a 36 in opening, and that excess is the style's argument.

exceptions.why: The Federal casing is deliberately narrower than the Georgian, and the pack tests that as an invariant; Adamesque delicacy is the point.
exceptions.bounds: Narrower than Georgian but still within Palladio's band at opening / 6 or a shade under, and compensated by finer profiles, reeding and applied composition ornament. Federal narrowness is refinement, not omission.

bounds_test.note: Narrower than Georgian but still inside Palladio's band, compensated by finer profiles, reeding and applied composition ornament. Federal narrowness is refinement, not omission, and below 0.15 it is omission.

exceptions.why: Flat broad boards in a single dark value, with contrast doing the work that profile does elsewhere.
exceptions.bounds: Not less than 5 in wide. The idiom's licence is on profile, not on width — narrow flat trim in this idiom reads as builder-grade and the style's own diagnostic is the two-value contrast, which needs area to work.

bounds_test.note: THE LINE, STATED. The licence is on profile, not on width. 5 to 7 in flat boards in a strict second value against the wall; below 5 in neither shadow nor contrast is working.

applies_when.note: A contemporary idiom; the licence does not transfer to a revival of an earlier style.

confused_with.difference: Width of the band versus presence of the cap above it. A correct 6 in casing with no crown is still the other fault.
That fault is a mismatch between a door and a surround kit; this is a general undersizing of the trim band on any opening.

That fault is about how flat casing is joined at the head — mitred like a picture frame rather than butted under a head board. It is a Craftsman-specific assembly error; this is a universal width error, and a correctly wide casing can still be mitred wrong.

sources: Palladio, I quattro libri, Book I ch. XXVI
Asher Benjamin, The American Builder's Companion (1806)

test.note: Palladio permits 1/6 to 1/5 of the void, that is 0.167 to 0.20. 0.15 is the tolerance floor. The stock 2 1/4 in casing on a 36 in opening gives 0.06 — modern practice misses this by roughly a factor of three. Greek Revival deliberately exceeds 0.20, so the upper bound is a style question and only the floor is universal.

secondary_tests.note: Projection is about 0.18 of the casing width, roughly 1 in on a 6 in casing, which normally means a backband. Width without projection is only half the rule, and a flat outer edge meeting the wall with no step means the second half is unmet.

The window casing in a given room is WIDER than the door casing in the same room — opening/5.5 against opening/6 — because the window is the thing being framed and the door is the thing being passed through. Identical casings mean the trim was bought rather than composed.

severity_by_style.why: The style refuses casing almost entirely; its constraint caps it at 3 in and 1 in of projection.
Broad flat trim is the style's method and its casing deliberately exceeds Palladio's upper bound; a narrow casing here removes the ornament-by-mass argument the style is making.
The Federal casing is deliberately narrower than the Georgian and the pack tests that ordering as an invariant; Adamesque delicacy is the point, so the floor matters more than the target.
The type caps window casing at 4 to 5 in as a deliberate budget that must read as a budget.
The idiom's whole diagnostic is a two-value contrast, and contrast needs area; narrow flat trim reads as builder-grade and there is no profile to fall back on.

inverted_by.statement: Casing over 3 in wide or 1 in proud is the fault. Openings must read as punched rather than framed, and a Palladian architrave on a shingle wall is the error.
An individual casing is the fault; the opening is bounded by continuous lintel and sill bands and an applied architrave interrupts them.
